prompt: A team is applying the Reliability pillar to a Bedrock-based application that calls foundation models. Which TWO patterns improve resilience to FM call failures and regional issues? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Disable retries to reduce latency
options.explanation: Removing retries reduces, not improves, resilience to transient failures.

options.text: Increase the model temperature to add response variety
options.explanation: Temperature affects output randomness, not reliability.

options.text: Implement circuit breakers in an AWS Step Functions workflow that stop calling the FM when error rates spike
Configure cross-Region failover so requests shift to a healthy Region
Store all prompts in a single Amazon S3 bucket in one Region
options.explanation: A single-Region store is a single point of failure, the opposite of resilient design.

explanation: Circuit breakers prevent cascading failures by halting calls to a failing dependency. Cross-Region failover keeps the workload available during a regional impairment. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A platform team wants to track and attribute Bedrock inference costs per internal team while using cross-Region inference. Which capability lets them tag usage for cost tracking?

options.text: Provisioned Throughput model units
options.explanation: Model Units reserve capacity; they are not the per-team tagging mechanism for cross-Region inference.

options.text: System-defined inference profiles, which you create and tag yourself
options.explanation: System-defined profiles are predefined by AWS and are not user-tagged; application profiles are the taggable, custom ones.

options.text: Application inference profiles, which are user-created and support tagging for cost allocation
AWS Cost Anomaly Detection profiles
options.explanation: That detects spend anomalies; it does not create taggable inference routing profiles.

explanation: Application inference profiles are custom profiles you create and tag, enabling cost tracking; system-defined profiles are AWS-managed. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt: A team is choosing between Amazon Comprehend and Amazon Macie for handling PII. Which guidance is correct?

options.text: Use Comprehend to scan an entire S3 lake for sensitive data classification
options.explanation: Lake-wide discovery/classification is Macie's role.

options.text: Use Comprehend to detect/redact PII in text you process; use Macie to discover/classify sensitive data across S3
Use Macie to redact PII inside chatbot prompts in real time
options.explanation: Macie is a discovery/classification service for S3, not a real-time text redactor.

options.text: They are interchangeable for all PII tasks
options.explanation: They serve different purposes and are not interchangeable.

explanation: Comprehend redacts text content; Macie is for S3-wide sensitive-data discovery and posture. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A diagnostic app stores 50 million image embeddings and runs similarity searches only occasionally, wanting the most cost-effective, serverless option with no infrastructure to manage. Which vector store is best?

options.text: Amazon OpenSearch Serverless
options.explanation: OpenSearch Serverless targets high query rates and low-latency search; for a large corpus that is rarely queried, S3 Vectors is the cost-optimized store.

options.text: Amazon DynamoDB with custom Lambda search
options.explanation: Custom search logic in Lambda is code to build and run. DynamoDB now has native vector search, but it is aimed at real-time, single-digit-millisecond lookups rather than lowest-cost storage for rarely queried vectors.

options.text: Amazon Aurora PostgreSQL pgvector
options.explanation: Aurora requires managing a database instance and is not cost-optimal for infrequent workloads.

options.text: Amazon S3 Vectors

explanation: S3 Vectors is purpose-built, cost-optimized vector storage with no infrastructure to provision, and it is ideal for workloads where queries are infrequent. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/AmazonS3/latest/userguide/s3-vectors.html

prompt: A team is deciding chunk size. What is the typical trade-off between very large and very small chunks?

options.text: Smaller chunks always retrieve better in every case
options.explanation: Too-small chunks can lose needed context.

options.text: Large chunks preserve context but can dilute relevance and exceed limits; small chunks are precise but may lose surrounding context
Larger chunks always reduce cost
options.explanation: Larger chunks can increase tokens per retrieval and cost.

options.text: Chunk size has no effect on retrieval quality
options.explanation: Chunk size materially affects relevance and context.

explanation: Chunk size trades context retention against retrieval precision and token limits. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-chunking.html

prompt: A team wants more deterministic, focused output from a model for a compliance-sensitive summarization task. Which parameter change is most appropriate?

options.text: Lower the temperature toward 0
Raise the temperature near maximum
options.explanation: High temperature increases randomness, the opposite of deterministic.

options.text: Add more stop sequences to increase creativity
options.explanation: Stop sequences end generation; they do not control creativity.

options.text: Increase max_tokens to reduce randomness
options.explanation: max_tokens affects length, not determinism.

explanation: Lower temperature reduces randomness, producing more deterministic, focused output. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: A team must deploy existing Python agent code to Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Runtime with minimal overhead. It must auto-handle the HTTP server, /invocations and /ping endpoints, and support both sub-second and streaming responses. Which TWO approaches fit best? (Select all that apply.)

options.text: Hand-build a FastAPI server with custom /invocations and /ping and your own container orchestration
options.explanation: Manual server and orchestration work is the overhead AgentCore is meant to remove.

options.text: Deploy on a SageMaker real-time endpoint with a custom inference container
options.explanation: A custom inference container adds infrastructure work AgentCore avoids.

options.text: Deploy on Amazon ECS Fargate with a fully custom container image and task definitions
options.explanation: Custom ECS deployment increases operational overhead versus AgentCore's managed flow.

options.text: Use the AgentCore CLI (`agentcore create`, `agentcore deploy`) to package the code (CodeZip by default, or a container build) and deploy it to AgentCore Runtime
Use the AgentCore Python SDK (`BedrockAgentCoreApp` with the @app.entrypoint decorator) so the required endpoints are handled for you

explanation: `agentcore deploy` packages the code into a zip artifact uploaded to Amazon S3 (the default CodeZip build type, which needs no Docker) or builds a container, then creates the AgentCore Runtime endpoint. Wrapping the agent with the AgentCore Python SDK satisfies the Runtime HTTP contract: port 8080, POST `/invocations` returning JSON or SSE streaming responses, and GET `/ping`. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock-agentcore/latest/devguide/runtime-get-started-cli.html

prompt:
A museum archive's RAG assistant uses Amazon Bedrock Knowledge Bases. Researchers submit multi-intent questions that compare preservation guidance across several media types, and profiling shows a single retrieval call often finds evidence for one part of the question but misses the others. The application already generates the final answer with its own separate model invocation because it must inject a strict JSON response schema and review metadata.

Which approach improves retrieval coverage for these questions?

options.text: Raise the generation model's temperature so it is more likely to cover all parts of the question.
options.explanation: Generation cannot cover evidence that was never retrieved.

options.text: Replace the custom generation step with RetrieveAndGenerate and drop the JSON schema requirement.
options.explanation: The scenario needs the custom generation step for the JSON schema and metadata.

options.text: Add a step that decomposes the question into sub-queries, call the knowledge base Retrieve operation for each sub-query, merge and de-duplicate the retrieved contexts, and pass them to the existing generation prompt.
Increase the embedding dimension so a single query vector can represent several intents at once.
options.explanation: Dimensionality does not let one vector target several distinct topics.

explanation: Multi-part questions produce one query vector that lands between the sub-topics; decomposing into focused sub-queries and retrieving for each one recovers evidence for every part, and because the application owns generation, the merged contexts feed its existing structured prompt. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-retrieve.html

prompt:
A field-service RAG assistant uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base on Amazon OpenSearch Serverless; the vector index stores each chunk's raw text in a filterable text field. Technicians search with natural-language symptoms and with exact robot model numbers or error codes. Profiling shows semantic retrieval often misses chunks that contain the exact code, and relevant chunks sometimes rank below less useful ones. The team wants better relevance from Retrieve and RetrieveAndGenerate with configuration changes only.

Which change meets these requirements?

options.text: In the retrieval configuration, override the search type to hybrid so keyword matching on the text field is combined with vector similarity, raise the number of results, and add a reranking configuration that uses an Amazon Bedrock reranker model to reorder the candidates.
Reduce the number of results to one so that only the single best chunk is passed to the model.
options.explanation: Makes misses worse by cutting recall to a single chunk.

options.text: Ask technicians to describe the error in words instead of typing the code.
options.explanation: A workaround that discards the most precise signal users have.

options.text: Switch the embedding model to one with more dimensions so exact codes are represented more precisely.
options.explanation: Dimensionality does not make an embedding model match exact tokens, and it forces a full re-embed.

explanation: Hybrid search adds lexical matching, which finds exact identifiers that dense vectors represent poorly, and a reranker model rescoring a larger candidate set fixes the ordering problem; both are retrieval configuration settings, with no re-indexing. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt:
A medical device manufacturer's AI governance office already uses AWS Audit Manager for internal control evidence. It is standardizing oversight for several foundation model applications on Amazon Bedrock and Amazon SageMaker AI. The programme must align with responsible AI principles, support both automated and manually collected evidence, and must not present the results as a formal compliance certification.

Which approach meets these requirements with the LEAST custom governance work?

options.text: Run Amazon SageMaker Clarify on every model and file the bias reports as the governance evidence.
options.explanation: Bias metrics are one piece of evidence, not a governance framework.

options.text: Write a custom control set from scratch in a spreadsheet and ask each team to self-attest quarterly.
options.explanation: The most custom work and no automated evidence.

options.text: Create an AWS Audit Manager assessment from the prebuilt AWS generative AI best practices framework, collect automated evidence where supported, and attach manual evidence for procedural controls.
Enable AWS Config conformance packs for HIPAA and treat a passing score as generative AI certification.
options.explanation: Config rules check resource configuration, not generative AI practices, and are not a certification either.

explanation: Audit Manager ships a prebuilt generative AI best practices framework whose controls map to responsible AI principles; an assessment from it collects automated evidence from supported services and accepts manual evidence uploads, and Audit Manager assessments are explicitly not certifications. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/audit-manager/latest/userguide/aws-generative-ai-best-practices.html

prompt:
An insurance claims assistant invokes Amazon Bedrock from a Lambda function. After the team added a model from a different provider and later an imported custom model, some requests fail with a validation error saying required fields are missing, and other requests succeed but ignore several generation settings such as the maximum output length. The team must keep using the InvokeModel API and keep the client request contract unchanged.

Which change should the team make?

options.text: Add a model-aware serialization layer in the Lambda function that sets the content type to application/json and converts the internal request into the documented native request body and parameter names for each model ID.
Purchase Provisioned Throughput for the new models so that validation is relaxed for dedicated capacity.
options.explanation: Capacity has no effect on request validation.

options.text: Send the same JSON body to every model and set the inference parameters as HTTP headers instead.
options.explanation: Bedrock reads inference parameters from the body, not headers.

options.text: Increase the Lambda function's memory and timeout so the model has enough resources to accept the request.
options.explanation: The errors are schema mismatches, not resource limits.

explanation: InvokeModel request and response bodies are model-specific: each provider defines its own field names and parameter names, so a body that works for one model is missing required fields for another and silently ignores unknown settings. A translation layer per model ID fixes both symptoms while the client contract stays stable. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-parameters.html

prompt:
A financial institution's platform team is building a centralized GenAI gateway that internal applications must use to reach Amazon Bedrock. The gateway must enforce request validation and throttling, keep an audit trail of model access, and be released through an automated pipeline that includes security checks. If a release raises errors or latency, it must roll back automatically.

Which solution meets these requirements with the LEAST operational overhead?

options.text: Deploy the gateway on an Auto Scaling group of EC2 instances behind an Application Load Balancer and update the AMI by hand after each code review.
options.explanation: No automated rollback and the most to operate.

options.text: Deploy the gateway as Amazon API Gateway with usage plans and request validation in front of a Lambda function that invokes Bedrock. Use AWS CodePipeline with CodeBuild for tests and security scans, deploy the function with AWS CodeDeploy canary traffic shifting on a Lambda alias, attach CloudWatch alarms that trigger automatic rollback, and enable AWS CloudTrail and CloudWatch Logs for auditing.
Give every application its own IAM role with direct Bedrock access and rely on CloudTrail as the gateway.
options.explanation: There is no gateway to enforce validation or throttling.

options.text: Deploy the Lambda function with an all-at-once update and ask the on-call engineer to redeploy the previous version if errors rise.
options.explanation: Rollback is manual and every user hits the bad version.

explanation: API Gateway provides validation, throttling via usage plans and access logs; CodePipeline with CodeBuild runs tests and scans; CodeDeploy shifts a small share of traffic to the new Lambda version and rolls back automatically when an alarm fires; CloudTrail records the Bedrock API calls. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/codedeploy/latest/userguide/deployment-configurations.html

prompt:
A product team has launched an internal chat assistant for support agents on Amazon Bedrock. The team wants a user-centred way to keep improving response quality by collecting a per-response rating and optional written feedback, and later analysing that feedback by model and prompt version. The solution must be serverless and require the LEAST operational overhead.

Which solution meets these requirements?

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock human-based evaluation job after each release and have the support agents act as the work team.
options.explanation: That is a batch, offline rating of a fixed dataset, not continuous in-product feedback on live responses.

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging and ask agents to type their rating into the next chat message so it appears in the logs.
options.explanation: It pollutes the conversation, sends the rating to the model, and leaves no structured record.

options.text: Add a "Rate this answer" control to the web UI that calls an Amazon API Gateway endpoint. Use an AWS Lambda function to validate the request and store the rating, free-text feedback, model ID, and prompt version in an Amazon DynamoDB table for later analysis.
Run an Amazon EC2 instance with a relational database and a REST service that receives ratings from the UI.
options.explanation: It works but is not serverless and carries patching and scaling overhead.

explanation: API Gateway, Lambda and DynamoDB form a fully serverless feedback path, and storing the model ID and prompt version with each rating makes the later per-version analysis a simple query. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/services-apigateway.html

prompt: A security team is hardening a Bedrock workload according to the Security pillar of the Generative AI Lens. Which TWO practices should they adopt? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Send prompts to a public endpoint without TLS to reduce overhead.
options.explanation: Unencrypted transport exposes sensitive prompt and response data.

options.text: Embed long-lived IAM access keys in the application package.
options.explanation: Long-lived embedded keys are a major security risk and violate credential best practices.

options.text: Encrypt data at rest with AWS KMS and reach Bedrock through VPC endpoints to keep traffic on the AWS network.
Apply least-privilege IAM with condition keys (for example, requiring a specific bedrock:GuardrailIdentifier) for model access.
Disable all logging to minimize the data footprint.
options.explanation: Disabling logging removes the audit trail needed for security monitoring and compliance.

explanation: Customer-managed encryption and private connectivity protect data confidentiality and reduce exposure of prompts and outputs. Least-privilege identity-based policies with condition keys restrict who can call models and can enforce that guardrails are applied. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/wellarchitected/latest/generative-ai-lens/generative-ai-lens.html

prompt: A team is preparing a dataset to fine-tune a foundation model and wants to maximize resulting quality while avoiding overfitting and data leakage. Which TWO data-preparation steps best support these goals? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Include duplicate records to increase the dataset size.
options.explanation: Duplication inflates size artificially and encourages overfitting to repeated examples.

options.text: Increase the number of training epochs regardless of validation loss.
options.explanation: Blindly adding epochs is a training hyperparameter choice, not data preparation, and risks overfitting.

options.text: Include PII in the examples to add more signal.
options.explanation: Including PII creates privacy and compliance risk and does not improve task quality.

options.text: Hold out a separate validation/test split that does not overlap the training data.
Deduplicate and clean/normalize the examples.

explanation: A non-overlapping evaluation split prevents train/test leakage and gives an honest measure of generalization. Removing duplicates and normalizing inconsistent text reduces bias toward repeated samples and improves the signal the model learns from. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/data-wrangler.html

prompt: A team wants to A/B test two wordings of a production prompt and roll back instantly if one underperforms, without redeploying application code. Which Amazon Bedrock capability supports this?

options.text: Hard-code both prompts in the application and redeploy to switch.
options.explanation: Hard-coding requires a code change and redeploy for every switch or rollback.

options.text: Amazon Bedrock Prompt Management with versioned prompts and variants.
Store prompts in environment variables only.
options.explanation: Environment variables lack versioning, variants, and managed rollback for prompts.

options.text: Change the temperature parameter to switch prompts.
options.explanation: Temperature does not select between prompt wordings.

explanation: Prompt Management stores prompts as versioned, parameterized resources with variants, so teams can compare wordings and switch or roll back without code changes. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prompt-management.html

prompt: An agent should ground its answers in the company's policy documents in addition to taking actions. With the LEAST custom code, how should the developer add this knowledge?

options.text: Associate an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base with the agent.
Fine-tune the agent's model on the policies each week.
options.explanation: Repeated fine-tuning is heavy and unnecessary when a knowledge base provides current grounding.

options.text: Embed the entire policy library into the agent's instructions.
options.explanation: Instructions have limited size and cannot scale to a full document library or stay current.

options.text: Store policies in DynamoDB and query them with custom code.
options.explanation: A custom store and retrieval code adds work that the built-in knowledge base association avoids.

explanation: Associating a knowledge base lets the agent retrieve and ground responses on the documents without custom retrieval code. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/agents.html

prompt: A team must retain the full request and response content of every Amazon Bedrock model call for troubleshooting and audit. Which capability captures this with the LEAST custom code?

options.text: Use Amazon Macie on the application logs.
options.explanation: Macie classifies sensitive data; it does not capture model request/response content.

options.text: Enable AWS CloudTrail only.
options.explanation: CloudTrail records API activity metadata, not the full prompt and response content.

options.text: Add print statements in the application and hope they are captured.
options.explanation: Ad hoc logging is incomplete and unreliable compared with built-in invocation logging.

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging to Amazon S3 (and/or CloudWatch Logs).

explanation: Model invocation logging is a built-in feature that records full prompts, responses, and metadata to S3 and/or CloudWatch with no custom instrumentation. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-invocation-logging.html

prompt: A production Bedrock workload has steady, high, predictable demand for 12 business hours and near-zero traffic overnight. The team must guarantee dedicated capacity during business hours (no throttling) at the lowest total cost, keeping the same model and API. Which approach is BEST?

options.text: Use Provisioned Throughput without a long-term commitment, creating model units for business hours and deleting them overnight.
Use on-demand inference for all traffic.
options.explanation: On-demand has no idle cost but cannot guarantee dedicated capacity during peak hours, so it fails the no-throttling requirement.

options.text: Use Provisioned Throughput with a 6-month commitment sized for peak.
options.explanation: A committed term has the most discounted hourly price, but it cannot be deleted until the term ends, so you pay for the units overnight too.

options.text: Use cross-Region inference to add capacity during business hours.
options.explanation: Cross-Region inference routes on-demand traffic across Regions for throughput but does not reserve guaranteed capacity.

explanation: No-commitment Provisioned Throughput can be deleted at any time and is billed hourly until it is deleted, so creating it for business hours and deleting it overnight gives dedicated capacity without paying for the idle period. Status note: Provisioned Throughput can be purchased only for the models on its supported list (Amazon Nova, Amazon Titan, older Anthropic Claude 3 models, Llama 3.1/3.2 and some embedding models), so this pattern applies only to models that still support it. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/prov-throughput.html

prompt: A bank's assistant must always cite the LATEST internal regulations (which change weekly) AND must CONSISTENTLY emit a strict report template. Which approach meets BOTH with the least ongoing effort?

options.text: Fine-tune the model every week on both the regulations and the template.
options.explanation: Weekly fine-tuning is operationally heavy and still lags between runs; RAG handles freshness far more cheaply.

options.text: Use RAG only, relying on a detailed prompt to enforce the template.
options.explanation: RAG fixes freshness, but prompt-only formatting is not reliably consistent, which the scenario explicitly requires.

options.text: Use continued pre-training on the regulations and a prompt for the template.
options.explanation: Continued pre-training is for absorbing domain language from large corpora, is heavy, and does not keep weekly content current.

options.text: Use RAG for the frequently changing regulations and fine-tune the model for the fixed report template/style.

explanation: RAG keeps regulatory content current without retraining, while fine-tuning reliably enforces a rigid output format; each technique handles the part it is best at. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/model-cards.html

prompt:
A maritime logistics team is building an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base from vessel maintenance manuals in Amazon S3. Users ask natural-language questions and must be able to narrow retrieval by vessel class, manual revision date, subsystem, and document owner. The team wants to avoid custom ingestion code and keep the attributes associated with each source document.

Which implementation meets these requirements?

options.text: Create one knowledge base per vessel class, subsystem, and owner combination and pick the right one at query time.
options.explanation: A combinatorial explosion of knowledge bases to maintain.

options.text: Write a custom Lambda ingestion pipeline that stores the attributes in DynamoDB and post-filters the retrieved chunks.
options.explanation: The custom code the team wants to avoid, and post-filtering throws away results after the top-k cut.

options.text: Place a metadata sidecar file next to each document in S3, named with the document's file name plus the .metadata.json suffix, containing the attributes; after ingestion, pass a metadata filter in the retrieval configuration of Retrieve or RetrieveAndGenerate calls.
Prepend the attributes as a header line inside each document so they are embedded with the content, and ask the model to ignore results from the wrong vessel class.
options.explanation: The attributes become part of the embedded text and cannot be used as exact filters; asking the model to ignore results is unreliable.

explanation: Bedrock knowledge bases read a per-document metadata JSON sidecar during ingestion and store the attributes with every chunk from that document, so retrieval calls can filter on them without any custom ingestion code. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/kb-test-config.html

prompt:
A clinical operations platform ingests partner trial-site notes as JSON into Amazon S3, normalizes them, and creates embeddings for an Amazon Bedrock RAG application. The JSON contains nested structures, and records that fail completeness and uniqueness checks must be quarantined before the curated dataset is loaded for embedding. Rule pass and fail counts must be published to CloudWatch for alarms, with minimal custom validation code.

Which validation design BEST meets these requirements?

options.text: Run Amazon Macie on the bucket to find incomplete records.
options.explanation: It discovers sensitive data; it does not validate completeness or uniqueness.

options.text: Add an AWS Glue ETL validation stage that flattens the nested fields, evaluates an AWS Glue Data Quality ruleset written in DQDL for completeness and uniqueness, publishes the rule results as CloudWatch metrics, and writes passing records to the curated prefix and failing records to a quarantine prefix.
Send every record to the foundation model and ask it to decide whether the record is complete.
options.explanation: Slow, expensive and non-deterministic for a structural check.

options.text: Write a Lambda function with hand-coded checks for each field and log the failures to CloudWatch Logs.
options.explanation: The custom validation code the team wants to minimize, and logs are not metrics.

explanation: Glue Data Quality evaluates declarative DQDL rules (such as IsComplete and IsUnique) inside a Glue job, can emit per-rule results as CloudWatch metrics, and row-level outcomes let the job route records to curated or quarantine outputs. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/glue/latest/dg/glue-data-quality.html

prompt:
A utility's grid reliability team is building an Amazon Bedrock based assistant that recommends restoration actions during outages. Each request can go through several plan, tool-call, and revise cycles; the tools are Lambda functions that read operational APIs. Safety reviewers require the workflow to stop after a fixed maximum number of cycles or after a high-risk tool result, to prevent the model path from reaching anything except approved read-only APIs, and to stop calling an unhealthy API for several minutes after consecutive failures. Auditors must be able to review every step.

Which design meets these requirements?

options.text: Build a Standard AWS Step Functions workflow that tracks the cycle count and risk flags with Choice and Fail states, invokes the Lambda tool adapters with timeouts, stores circuit-breaker state with a TTL in DynamoDB that the workflow checks before each call, and gives each adapter a least-privilege IAM role scoped to its read API.
Let a Strands agent run the loop in a single Lambda function with no step limit, relying on the model to decide when to stop and on Lambda's timeout as the safety net.
options.explanation: The model deciding when to stop does not satisfy a hard maximum, and Lambda's timeout is not a safety control.

options.text: Use an Amazon Bedrock agent with one action group whose Lambda role has full access to the operational APIs so any needed call can be made.
options.explanation: Violates least privilege and the read-only requirement.

options.text: Run the loop in an Amazon ECS task that retries failed APIs immediately until they recover.
options.explanation: Hammering an unhealthy API is the opposite of a cooldown.

explanation: Step Functions gives an explicit, auditable execution history with deterministic loop control (a counter with Choice states and a Fail state for unsafe outcomes), native timeouts and retries, and a place to check a DynamoDB circuit-breaker flag before each tool call; per-adapter IAM roles enforce the read-only boundary. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/step-functions/latest/dg/connect-bedrock.html

prompt:
A browser-based writing coach calls a Lambda function that invokes Amazon Bedrock synchronously, so students wait for the whole answer before seeing any feedback. The browser client already supports server-sent events, and the team does not want to adopt a WebSocket protocol. The solution must reduce time to first byte and stream partial model output as it is generated.

Which implementation meets these requirements?

options.text: Keep the synchronous call but lower maxTokens so the full answer arrives sooner.
options.explanation: A shorter answer is still delivered all at once, and it truncates feedback.

options.text: Have the browser poll a DynamoDB-backed endpoint every second for partial output written by the function.
options.explanation: Adds latency, cost and complexity compared with a streamed response.

options.text: Invoke the model with ConverseStream in the function, buffer all chunks, and return the concatenated text when the stream ends.
options.explanation: Consuming ConverseStream but returning only at the end gives the client nothing until completion.

options.text: Enable Lambda response streaming for the function (RESPONSE_STREAM invoke mode on a function URL or a streaming-capable HTTP front end), call ConverseStream, and write a server-sent event for each content delta as it arrives.

explanation: Lambda response streaming lets the function write bytes to the client progressively, so each ConverseStream delta can be flushed as an SSE frame and the first tokens reach the browser almost immediately. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/lambda/latest/dg/configuration-response-streaming.html

prompt:
A biomedical imaging vendor is deploying a 70 GB open-weight LLM from Amazon S3 to an Amazon SageMaker AI real-time endpoint for interactive report drafting. Endpoint creation repeatedly fails because downloading the artifact and passing the container startup health check take too long, and the chosen GPU instance's local storage is too small for the full artifact. The team also wants a serving stack designed for LLM memory use and token throughput.

Which deployment configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Switch to SageMaker Serverless Inference so that no instance storage is needed.
options.explanation: It does not support GPU instances, which an LLM of this size needs.

options.text: Deploy with a SageMaker Large Model Inference (LMI) container. Point the model at the uncompressed S3 prefix through ModelDataSource with compression type None, and on the production variant set VolumeSizeInGB, ModelDataDownloadTimeoutInSeconds, and ContainerStartupHealthCheckTimeoutInSeconds large enough for the artifact.
Deploy with a generic scikit-learn container and increase the instance count to spread the download across instances.
options.explanation: Each instance still downloads the whole model, and the container cannot serve an LLM efficiently.

options.text: Compress the weights into a single model.tar.gz, keep the default timeouts, and retry endpoint creation until it succeeds.
options.explanation: Extraction of a huge tarball makes startup slower and the timeouts still trip.

explanation: The LMI container is built for LLM serving (tensor parallelism, paged attention, continuous batching); an uncompressed model data source avoids a long tar extraction, VolumeSizeInGB provides enough attached storage, and the download and health-check timeouts stop SageMaker declaring the container unhealthy while 70 GB of weights load. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/sagemaker/latest/dg/large-model-inference.html

prompt:
A digital bank's customer-facing assistant on Amazon Bedrock has failed red-team testing: harmful language appeared in both prompts and responses, and testers attempted jailbreaks and prompt leakage. Compliance requires blocking harmful content when the guardrail classifies it as medium or high confidence while allowing low-confidence matches to limit false positives, observing prompt-attack detections for 30 days before changing user-visible behaviour, and anonymizing PII in responses.

Which guardrail configuration meets these requirements?

options.text: Create a guardrail with every content filter at high strength, the prompt attack filter blocking, and PII set to block, so that nothing harmful can get through.
options.explanation: High strength blocks low-confidence matches too (more false positives), and blocking prompt attacks changes user-visible behaviour immediately.

options.text: Rely on Amazon Comprehend toxicity detection in a Lambda function and skip Bedrock Guardrails to avoid added latency.
options.explanation: It covers toxicity but not prompt attacks, response filtering or PII masking in one place.

options.text: Create an Amazon Bedrock guardrail with the hate, insults, sexual, violence, and misconduct content filters set to medium strength for both prompts and responses, the prompt attack filter set to detect rather than block, and the sensitive information filter set to mask PII in responses.
Add a denied topic called "harmful content" and a word filter for known jailbreak phrases, and leave PII handling to the model's system prompt.
options.explanation: Denied topics are for subjects, not toxicity categories, and a phrase list does not catch novel jailbreaks or mask PII.

explanation: Content filter strength controls which confidence levels are blocked: medium strength blocks medium and high confidence classifications and lets low confidence through. The prompt attack filter can be set to detect, which records detections without intervening, giving the 30-day observation window, and the sensitive information filter's mask action anonymizes PII in text responses. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/guardrails-content-filters.html

prompt:
A financial services firm wants its developers to build proof-of-concept applications that call Amazon Bedrock from local Python scripts. The firm uses Okta for workforce identity and requires single sign-on with short-lived credentials and no long-term access keys. Developers must be able to run inference against approved foundation models but must not be able to manage models, agents, or knowledge bases.

Which solution provides the MOST secure, least-privilege access?

options.text: Create one IAM user per developer with an access key and attach the AmazonBedrockFullAccess managed policy.
options.explanation: Long-term credentials, and full access violates least privilege.

options.text: Create a shared IAM role with full Bedrock access and distribute its long-lived credentials through a password manager.
options.explanation: Shared long-lived secrets are the opposite of the requirement.

options.text: Connect AWS IAM Identity Center to Okta as the identity provider. Create a permission set for the developer group with a custom policy that allows only Bedrock Runtime actions such as InvokeModel and Converse on the approved model ARNs, and have developers obtain temporary credentials through Identity Center for the AWS SDK.
Use Amazon Cognito user pools for the developers and attach a policy that allows all Bedrock actions.
options.explanation: Cognito is for application end users rather than workforce SSO, and the policy is over-broad.

explanation: Identity Center federates with Okta, issues short-lived credentials for CLI and SDK sessions, and its permission sets carry a least-privilege policy that can be scoped to runtime invoke actions on specific model ARNs, leaving control-plane actions out. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/singlesignon/latest/userguide/what-is.html

prompt:
A SaaS support chat application uses the Amazon Bedrock Converse API with one foundation model. It stores the full conversation history in Amazon DynamoDB and uses an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base for RAG. As usage grows, Bedrock spend rises sharply and some requests fail because the prompt exceeds the model's context window. The company wants to reduce token-related cost while preserving answer quality.

Which combination of actions meets these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Increase the knowledge base's number of retrieved results so the model has more context and answers in fewer turns.
options.explanation: More chunks means more input tokens per request.

options.text: Store the conversation in Amazon S3 instead of DynamoDB to lower the per-request cost.
options.explanation: Storage location does not change model tokens.

options.text: Use a smaller, cheaper model to summarize older conversation turns into a running summary stored in DynamoDB, send only the summary plus the most recent turns, and cap the response with maxTokens.

Before each invocation, call CountTokens to measure the planned request; when it exceeds a budget, prune older turns and reduce the number of retrieved chunks, and publish input and output token counts to CloudWatch.
Switch to a model with a larger context window and send the entire history and all retrieved chunks on every request.
options.explanation: It removes the failure but raises cost further, which is the opposite of the goal.

explanation: Token cost is driven by what is sent to the model; measuring the request with CountTokens and trimming history and retrieved chunks to a budget, and compressing old turns into a short summary with a cheap model, both cut input tokens while keeping the relevant context. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/conversation-inference.html

prompt:
An insurance underwriting team is tuning the chunking and retrieval settings of an Amazon Bedrock knowledge base before wiring the retrieved content to a foundation model. The team needs a repeatable prerelease test that scores only the retrieval step against ground-truth answers written by subject matter experts, and wants request-level latency troubleshooting for the retrieval path without adding timing code to the application.

Which approach meets these requirements?

options.text: Run a retrieve-and-generate evaluation job and judge the final answers, then infer retrieval quality from the answer scores.
options.explanation: Answer quality mixes retrieval and generation effects, so it does not test the retrieval step on its own.

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging and review the logged prompts to see whether the right passages were included.
options.explanation: Logs show what was sent to the model, but they do not score retrieval or expose retrieval latency.

options.text: Add a Lambda function that times every Retrieve call and writes the duration to Amazon DynamoDB, and compare the top result with the expected answer by string match.
options.explanation: Custom timing code is exactly what the team wants to avoid, and string matching is a poor proxy for retrieval relevance.

options.text: Build a JSONL prompt dataset in Amazon S3 whose records contain the prompt and reference responses. Run a retrieve-only RAG evaluation job in Amazon Bedrock with context relevance and context coverage metrics, and use AWS X-Ray traces to analyze Retrieve latency.

explanation: Bedrock RAG evaluation jobs can be run in retrieve-only mode, where an evaluator model scores the retrieved contexts against the reference responses using metrics such as context relevance and context coverage, isolating the retriever from the generator. X-Ray traces the Retrieve calls made through the AWS SDK so per-request latency is visible without custom timers. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/bedrock/latest/userguide/evaluation-kb.html

prompt:
A telemedicine note-drafting service runs behind an Amazon API Gateway REST API; a Lambda function calls the Amazon Bedrock Converse API and currently logs only unstructured error strings. Support engineers spend hours correlating reports of wrong output, validation exceptions, and latency spikes. The team must improve triage across prompt versions, model invocations, and API hops, must not store raw patient data in logs, and must not introduce a separate observability data store.

Which TWO actions meet these requirements? (Select TWO.)

options.text: Enable Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging with full prompt and response bodies to CloudWatch Logs so every exchange is preserved for triage.
options.explanation: It would store raw patient data in logs, which the requirement forbids.

options.text: Increase the Lambda log retention to ten years so that older incidents can be reviewed.
options.explanation: Retention does not improve correlation or triage.

options.text: Emit structured JSON logs from the function with a correlation ID, prompt version, model ID, sanitized prompt and response attributes, latency, and validation outcome, and query them with CloudWatch Logs Insights.
Enable AWS X-Ray tracing on API Gateway and the Lambda function, instrument the AWS SDK client so Bedrock calls appear as subsegments, and include the trace ID in the application logs.
Ship all logs to a self-managed OpenSearch cluster and build Kibana dashboards for the support team.
options.explanation: That is the separate observability store the team must avoid.

explanation: X-Ray stitches API Gateway, Lambda and the downstream Bedrock call into one trace so latency can be attributed to a hop, and structured logs with a correlation ID, prompt version and model ID make Logs Insights queries answer "which version produced the bad output" without a new data store. Read more: https://docs.aws.amazon.com/xray/latest/devguide/aws-xray.html
